articles.title: Residents in China found three king cobra nests; scientists saw two cobras guarding one with 72 eggs
articles.summary: China News: Three king cobra nests discovered by residents in Yunnan, China, have given scientists an unusually close look at a part of the snakeâs life that rema.
articles.body: Three king cobra nests discovered by residents in Yunnan, China, have given scientists an unusually close look at a part of the snakeâs life that remains poorly documented. The nests, found between 2020 and 2025 in different parts of the province, contained 30, 72 and 25 eggs. The largest clutch, found west of Kunming, was particularly unexpected, with two king cobras observed guarding the same nest during several visits. Scientists could not establish the snakesâ sexes, leaving open the possibility that two females had contributed to the unusually large clutch. The other nests were found in bamboo forests, including one where young king cobras were later seen emerging. The observations are significant because they represent the first documented king cobra nesting and clutch-size records in China outside the Xizang Autonomous Region. The findings also add to growing evidence that the speciesâ nesting behaviour may be more varied than previously recorded. The observations are especially valuable because king cobras are difficult to study in the wild, and their reproductive behaviour is still not fully understood. By documenting nest locations, egg numbers and parental behaviour, the findings provide rare details that can help researchers better understand how the species reproduces in different environments.Two king cobras guarded a nest near Kunming in 2024According to the study published in Integrative Conservation, titled âNovel Natural History Observations on the Reproductive Biology of King Cobra (Ophiophagus hannah) From Yunnan Province, Chinaâ, the first nest was found on 10 July 2020 in Menghai County, in Xishuangbanna Dai Autonomous Prefecture in southern Yunnan. Local residents came across it in a tropical bamboo forest at an elevation of about 1,730 metres. The nest was made largely from bamboo leaves and an adult king cobra was guarding it, believed by the researchers to be a female.Once the snake had moved away, the nest could be examined. Inside were 30 eggs, with developing embryos visible when the eggs were illuminated with a strong light. The observation was important because, before these records, documented information about king cobra nesting in China was largely confined to southeastern Xizang. The authors describe the three Yunnan observations as the first documented nesting and clutch-size records for the species in China outside that region.The second discovery was made several years later, on 6 June 2024, in a mixed forest west of Kunming. This time, residents found two king cobras at a nest made from pine needles. The snakes were still there when researchers returned on 1 July, with one measuring about 1.8 metres and the other more than 2 metres long.The nest itself was changing as the snakes continued working on it. By the July survey, it stood roughly 1 metre high and measured around 1.5 metres across. The researchers later found 72 eggs packed towards the centre of the structure. The eggs sat roughly half a metre above the ground and below the upper layer of nesting material. Temperatures inside the nest were estimated at between 35Â°C and 40Â°C, considerably warmer than the surrounding air.Scientists find new evidence of group guarding in king cobrasThe Kunming nest was unusual for another reason. Two king cobras were seen guarding it during the early observations, and both remained at the site during a second survey on 11 July. By 20 July, however, only the larger snake was still there. It eventually left the nest without incident when the researchers approached.The observation matters because the question of whether several king cobras can participate in guarding the same nest has remained uncertain. Older accounts had described both sexes taking part in nest guarding, but more recent field studies had not confirmed this behaviour. The authors say the Kunming observation provides new evidence that multiple individuals can participate in guarding a king cobra nest. They could not determine the sex of either snake, so the observation does not establish exactly how the two individuals were related or what role each played.The unusually large clutch found there made the situation even harder to explain. King cobra clutches reported in earlier studies have generally ranged from 14 to 37 eggs. Seventy-two eggs is far beyond that range and, according to the authors, is the largest clutch reported in published studies of Ophiophagus hannah in the strict sense.There are a couple of possibilities. The nest could have belonged to a single mating pair, with one female producing an exceptionally large clutch. The researchers also raise another explanation: two females may have nested together, combining their eggs in one nest. The fact that the 72 eggs were roughly twice the size of clutches recorded elsewhere lends some support to that idea, but the researchers stress that they could not determine the snakes' sexes. It remains a hypothesis rather than a conclusion.King cobra nest in Yunnan contained 25 eggsThe third nest was found in Lancang County, Pu'er City, south-central Yunnan, on 17 June 2025. Residents again made the initial discovery. They reported seeing two adult king cobras guarding the nest, although only one was present when the researchers visited.This nest was smaller than the one near Kunming. It had been built in a bamboo forest from bamboo leaves and twigs, measuring about 95 centimetres across at its base and roughly 50 centimetres high. Once the guarding snake left, researchers found 25 eggs inside, joined together as a single cluster. The temperature within the nest was about 26Â°C, the same as the surrounding air.The nest also offered something the other observations did not: a chance to see what happened after the eggs were laid. Juvenile king cobras were first observed emerging from the nest on 19 August 2025. That gave the researchers a direct record connecting the nesting site with successful hatching, adding another piece to an otherwise limited picture of reproduction in the species.The 25-egg clutch also sits comfortably within the range of previously recorded king cobra clutches. That makes the 72-egg Kunming nest stand out even more. Taken together, the three nests contained 30, 72 and 25 eggs, showing how much clutch size can vary between individual nesting events.King cobra nesting records help fill a geographical gap in ChinaKing cobras are unusual among snakes because they construct nests and guard their eggs. Yet despite being one of the world's best-known venomous snakes, their reproductive biology is still poorly documented across much of their range.The study notes that earlier work has been concentrated largely in the eastern Himalaya, where recorded clutches have ranged from 14 to 37 eggs. In China, the previous official nesting record came from southeastern Xizang. The Yunnan observations therefore fill an important geographical gap, particularly because they cover three separate nesting events in different parts of the province.The findings also need to be viewed in light of changes in how the species itself is classified. What was once treated as a single widespread king cobra species has more recently been considered a species complex containing four distinct species. The Ophiophagus hannah species in the study is now understood to occur in the Pan-Himalayan region, southern China and much of Indochina. It is listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN and as Endangered on China's Red List.For the researchers, the value of the Yunnan records is therefore not simply the discovery of three nests. The observations provide baseline information that can be compared with nesting behaviour elsewhere and may help determine whether the apparent group guarding and unusually large clutch in Kunming are rare exceptions or signs of behaviour that has simply gone undocumented.The authors say further fieldwork will be needed to test the competing explanations for the 72-egg nest. Whether it was produced by one unusually productive female or resulted from two females nesting together cannot be resolved from the observations available.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: âAttackers took bath, ate datesâ: Chilling details in Bangladesh Hindu family case
articles.summary: South Asia News: A Hindu family of four was found murdered inside their locked home in Bangladeshâs Rangpur city. Investigators said the suspects allegedly stayed at t.
articles.body: A Hindu family of four was found murdered inside their locked home in Bangladeshâs Rangpur city. Investigators said the suspects allegedly stayed at the house after the killings, bathed there, ate dates and cucumbers from the refrigerator and used yaba before fleeing, as per local media reports.The victims were identified as retired Rangpur Zilla School teacher Ganapati Chakraborty, 65, his wife Pritilata Chakraborty, 50, their daughter Agami Chakraborty Prarthi, 23, and their 12-year-old son Priyam Chakraborty. Their bodies were recovered from their home in the Daspara (Machhuapara) area at around 11.30pm on Saturday.According to Bangladeshâs Prothom Alo, Rangpur police commissioner Mohammad Abdul Mabud said two suspects, identified as Mugdha and Siddhartha, remained inside the house after the killings. Police said they left on Friday when the streets were relatively empty during Jummah prayers.Before leaving, the suspects allegedly opened cupboards and drawers and scattered clothes and other belongings around the house, apparently in an attempt to make the incident appear to be a robbery. articles.title: âMisguided actionsâ, Trump episode: Zelenskyy breaks silence on rift with sacked defence minister
articles.summary: Europe News: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has, for the first time, publicly detailed his dispute with ousted former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, w.
articles.body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has, for the first time, publicly detailed his dispute with ousted former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who has called for a wartime presidential election even as Ukraine remains under martial law due to the war with Russia, meaning fresh elections cannot be held under current conditions.The Ukrainian president made the remarks during an earlier off-the-record meeting with reporters, with a transcript of the discussion released publicly on Sunday (local time).Zelenskyy described some of Fedorovâs actions, including his calls for elections and involvement in mass protests, as âmisguided.ââI really had and still have a very positive attitude toward Mykhailo. We have been through a lot together. But I believe that he himself goes, or is pushed, into the wrong things,â the Ukrainian leader told reporters.Zelenskyy also appeared to link Fedorov to an episode involving Elon Musk and the billionaireâs Starlink satellite internet service. According to Zelenskyy, earlier this year, the Defence Ministry told him that SpaceX had agreed to allow Ukraine to use Starlink over Russian territory for deep-strike operations, subject to political approval.Acting on that information, Zelenskyy raised the issue directly with US President Donald Trump, telling him that Musk had confirmed the proposed use. The two sides subsequently sought confirmation from Musk and discussed financing for the project.Zelenskyy further stated that at a later meeting, Trump informed him that Musk had rejected the proposal and accused him of having âmisledâ the US president. Musk considered the move a âdangerous escalation,â he added.âHe (Trump) said that I had supposedly deceived him, because Musk had denied Ukraine the use of Starlink on Russian territory. I went back to our defence ministry, and they told me that maybe it was so,â Zelenskyy recalled.However, Zelenskyy stopped short of explicitly accusing Fedorov of lying, instead indicating that the episode was among the reasons behind âsome of the stepsâ he later took.Fedorov, a popular minister credited with modernizing Ukraineâs armed forces and accelerating the militaryâs embrace of technology and drone warfare, was dismissed last month after reportedly falling out with the countryâs top military commander. His removal triggered mass protests that lasted for weeks, but ultimately failed to force a reversal of the decision.Fedorov later called for an election.(With AP inputs)Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Southampton AI uncovers hidden clues in breast cancer
articles.summary: The findings could help doctors identify high-risk patients and develop more targeted treatments.
articles.body:
Researchers have developed an AI tool that reveals previously unseen patterns inside breast cancers.

A University of Southampton team, working with the city's hospital, used the technology to analyse more than 330,000 cells from 127 patients.

The findings could help doctors identify high-risk patients and develop more targeted treatments.

Leading the research, the university's Dr Salah Elias, said: "This opens the door to developing new biomarkers and, ultimately, more personalised treatment strategies."

The study found two different types of changes inside cancer cells that had previously been treated as the same thing.

One type involved cells developing too many centrosomes, which help cells divide properly. The other involved centrosomes becoming unusually large.

Researchers discovered the two changes could appear in different parts of the same tumour and may play different roles in how cancers develop.

The team created an AI platform, called CenSegNet, to examine tumour samples with "unprecedented speed and precision".

Centrosomes act as the cell's organising centres, helping cells divide and maintain their structure. When they become abnormal, cells can build up genetic mistakes, which are commonly seen in cancer.

The researchers found tumours with higher numbers of enlarged centrosomes were more likely to have features linked to more aggressive disease.

These included higher tumour grade, cancer that had spread to nearby lymph nodes and certain genetic changes.

The study also found patients with fewer enlarged centrosomes in the centre of their tumours tended to have better overall survival.

Elias, said: "For more than a century, centrosome abnormalities have been recognised as a hallmark of cancer, but studying them in patient tissues has been extremely challenging.

"CenSegNet allows us to analyse these defects at single-cell resolution across entire tumours and uncover patterns that were previously impossible to see."

Researchers say the technology could eventually help doctors better understand which cancers are more likely to grow, spread or resist treatment.

It could also help scientists develop more personalised treatments by identifying tumours with specific weaknesses that could be targeted with new drugs.

While the technology is not yet ready for routine use in hospitals, the team has also shown it can be used on tissue samples from other parts of the body, including the kidney, colon and appendix.

CenSegNet is available free of charge as open-source software, allowing researchers around the world to use and study the technology.

articles.title: Scottish National Investment Bank makes 'painful' Â£138m net loss
articles.summary: The publicly-owned body, which operates independently, has invested in several firms that collapsed last year.
articles.body:
The Scottish National Investment Bank has revealed it made a net loss of Â£138m last year.

The state-owned body cited the collapse of three of its early investments - including its first, Glasgow-based laser company M Squared.

However, the bank also generated an income of Â£32m, comfortably covering its operating costs of Â£20m.

Chairman Willie Watt called the losses "painful" but said the bank had learned lessons.

The Scottish National Investment Bank, which is independent from government, was set up by ministers in 2020 with a mission to fund business and innovation to boost economic growth.

Its report for the 2025-26 financial year , external revealed a net loss of Â£138m, including Â£65m of realised losses from the failure of three early investments - M Squared Lasers, the electric car charging firm Trojan Energy and the satellite and digital company Krucial.

There was a further Â£85m of unrealised losses after rocket manufacturer Orbex and medical technology firm Pneumowave entered administration.

The bank also invested a record Â£374m in Scottish ventures, while its operating costs were below budget.

Watt said: "The realised and unrealised losses we have seen in this financial year reflect that and are not where we want to be.

"While these figures are painful for the bank, they are particularly so for the businesses which failed and of course for their teams."

He cited a tough economic environment with "tighter financial conditions, cautious sentiment and more challenging fundraising".

Watt added: "We have learned a lot over the past five years and continue to improve and tighten our investment processes along with stricter criteria for potential investments as set out in our investment strategy."

Chief executive David Ritchie called the losses "regrettable and disappointing", but said he was determined to demonstrate that a "commercially disciplined development bank can deliver for Scotland".

Which companies backed by the bank have folded?

M Squared Lasers - the Glasgow technology firm was hailed by Nicola Sturgeon as "a great example of the ambitious and innovative companies we have here in Scotland" when the national investment bank was launched in 2020. It went into administration in 2025 with debts of Â£64m

Trojan Energy - the Aberdeen-based electric vehicle charging firm collapsed into administration with debt of almost Â£30m last year

Krucial - the Glasgow-based start-up, which specialised in satellite technology, folded last year.

Orbex - set up to run a planned satellite launch facility in the north-west Highlands, the company is to be liquidated and its assets sold off

Pneumowave - headquartered in Glasgow, the medical tech firm appointed liquidators in July

Since being set up in 2020, the bank has investment more than Â£1.2bn in 53 ventures and helped to raise Â£1.9bn in third-party investment.

An independent report by Sir John Elvidge , external , a former chief civil servant to the Scottish government, found that the bank was expected to have made losses of about Â£110m by the end of 2025-26 financial year.

He said it was important that the bank learned lessons from the losses, but did not say the scale of the failed investments were necessarily higher than should be expected for a newly launched body.

Responding to the bank's annual report, First Minister John Swinney said it must be able to take risks to deliver "greater economic returns".

He said that principle was essential to "constructing an economy that is fit for the 21st Century".

Scottish Labour economy spokesperson Daniel Johnson said: "These losses must be examined and the bank's leadership must continue to work to identify investment opportunities that will deliver for our economy and our communities."

Kim Schmulian, Reform UK Scotland's finance spokesperson, said: "This is yet another example of SNP ministers gambling with taxpayers' money while those responsible try to dress up failure as a 'challenging environment'."

Scottish Conservative finance spokesman Craig Hoy said that the bank "must not become another SNP vanity project where taxpayers are left to foot the bill for failure while ministers dodge responsibility".

articles.title: Hungarian Gripen fighter jet crashes: Pilot ejects safely, probe launched
articles.summary: Europe News: A Hungarian Air Force Gripen fighter jet crashed near the town of Szolnok on Monday, with the pilot successfully ejecting from the aircraft, prime min.
articles.body: A Hungarian Air Force Gripen fighter jet crashed near the town of Szolnok on Monday, with the pilot successfully ejecting from the aircraft, prime minister PÃ©ter Magyar said.The pilot survived and was taken to hospital, while no other injuries or damage to civilian infrastructure were reported.âFor reasons that are not yet known, a Gripen fighter jet of the Hungarian Defence Forces crashed a few minutes ago near Szolnok. The pilot successfully ejected. An investigation is under way, and the defence minister is on his way to the scene,â Magyar wrote on Facebook.Hungarian defence minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi later said the pilot had survived and was taken to hospital by ambulance.âThe pilot is in an ambulance, he is alive,â Ruszin-Szendi said in a Facebook video.The PM also said, âAccording to a preliminary report, there were no injuries and there was no harm in civilian infrastructure.âThe Hungarian army also has an air base near Szolnok. AP quoted Szolnok mayor MihÃ¡ly Gyorfi as saying the pilot âwas probably training as usualâ at the helicopter base outside the city, while confirming that there were no known injuries from the crash.Hungary, a NATO member, operates 18 JAS 39 Gripen fighter aircraft based at KecskemÃ©t. Fourteen were acquired through a lease-purchase programme launched in 2001, while four additional Gripens ordered in 2024 joined the fleet this year.The Hungarian Gripens regularly participate in international operations. In the second half of last year, the aircraft also took part in protecting the airspace of the Baltic states. The cause of Mondayâs crash remains unclear.Hungary previously experienced a Gripen accident in 2015, when a fighter crash-landed in central Hungary because of a technical fault. articles.title: UK missiles offer may help Ukraine - but they are not what Zelensky needs most
articles.summary: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham is handing over blueprints so Kyiv can build its own long-range missiles.
articles.body:
The UK is set to hand over blueprints for its British-French designed Storm Shadow cruise missiles to Ukraine â following a similar move from France â allowing Ukraine to produce the weapon domestically.

The move sends an important signal, showing that some Western nations are willing to share their expertise and know how to help Ukraine defend itself.

But, on its own, this won't dramatically alter the course of the war.

Scalp and Storm Shadow missiles have already been provided to Kyiv by both Britain and France. They've already been used to hit military targets inside Russia.

Burnham to hand long-range missile blueprints to Zelensky as he visits Kyiv Published 1 day ago

Burnham to hand long-range missile blueprints to Zelensky as he visits Kyiv

The weapons are not new â they were developed in the 1990s - and they are expensive â at around Â£1m a piece.

They also rely on complex global supply chains and have been built in peacetime at relatively low rates â in the hundreds, not the thousands.

Even with the blueprints, Ukraine may find it hard to source components. It could take months, possibly years to make the cruise missile themselves.

Copying Western weapons production in peacetime is, in fact, no way to win a war. Even Nato nations now realise that.

Britain and many of its allies have tended to produce small quantities of highly advanced, expensive missiles which would quickly run out in any protracted conflict.

In 2021, the former head of the US Army in Europe, Gen Ben Hodges, said that in a Nato wargame the UK military ran out of key weapons within a matter of days.

Proof of the recent change in mindset is the UK military is no longer buying Storm Shadow missiles for itself.

Instead, under Project Brakestop, it is developing its own long-range cruise missiles, free of foreign components, and less than half the price of a Storm Shadow.

Project Brakestop is also being done at break-neck speed. The UK hopes to have a new cruise missile ready by the end of the year. It is promising to supply the new weapon to Ukraine.

It is Ukraine which has shown the world how to produce relatively cheap, mass produced weapons, necessary for a long, protracted conflict.

Douglas Barrie, Senior Fellow for Military Aerospace at the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) told the BBC: "The decision to share UK classified information on the MBDA SCALP missiles with Ukraine, as France and Ukraine work toward local assembly lines in Ukraine, is notable. Any impact, however, will in part depend on how quickly Ukrainian assembled SCALP cruise missiles can be introduced into service.

"Given that Ukraine has already operated both Storm Shadow and SCALP, familiarity with the missile may help speed the overall process, but this will also be dependent on the extent and pace at which local assembly can be established."

At the start of the war its armed forces relied on old Cold War-era Soviet weaponry.

A slow supply of Western weapons helped it adapt. But now Ukraine produces 70% of its own weapons.

Key has been its rapid development of drone technology â from small First Person View (FPV) one-way attack drones for the front line, to larger long-range drones capable of striking deep into Russian territory, further than Storm Shadows can strike.

Kyiv is on track to build 10 million drones by the end of this year. And they can do it cheaper than the West, by using mass-produced Chinese parts.

Nato allies' equivalent drones can be twice as expensive as they try to shun Chinese components.

However, there are still weapons that Ukraine needs and struggles to produce on its own. From fast fighter jets to the most urgent example, interceptors to take down Russian ballistic missiles

The most effective weapon to do that, by far, is the US-made Patriot interceptor. Ukraine has all but run out of them and Russian ballistic missiles now make it through Ukrainian air defences with ease.

America's war in Iran has meant they're in even shorter supply.

They're also expensive â at around Â£3m a missile â and production rates have been slow. The US is planning to double production rates from around 600 Patriot missiles per annum to 2,000, but that will take several years.

President Donald Trump signalled last month that he would be willing to share Patriot technology with Ukraine, but has since rowed back .

Even if he had given approval, it would have taken a while for Ukraine to make Patriots themselves - some estimate at least a year. Ukraine would also be relying on the same sophisticated components that are in high demand across the globe.

Ukraine has embarked on a programme to develop its own interceptor missiles with European support â known as Project Freya.

But there are huge technological challenges in building a high-speed missile to take down another missile travelling at thousands of miles per hour. It is expensive and often time consuming.

Ukraine's military and its weapons manufacturers have shown themselves to be fast learners.

One of its own companies, Fire Point, is developing its own ballistic missiles which it hopes will be ready to fire in anger next year.

But Russia has already ramped up its own ballistic missile production, to around 100 a month.

Developing sophisticated weapons is expensive and cannot be done quickly. Ukraine is short of both time and money.

So, the move to hand missile blueprints to Ukraine will be welcome, but it is not an immediate fix for Ukraine's most pressing problems, and it wwill not dramatically alter Kyiv's ability to strike Russia in new ways.

The move sends an important signal, showing that some Western nations are willing to share their expertise and know how to help Ukraine defend itself.
But, on its own, this won't dramatically alter the course of the war.
Scalp and Storm Shadow missiles have already been provided to Kyiv by both Britain and France. They've already been used to hit military targets inside Russia.
Burnham to hand long-range missile blueprints to Zelensky as he visits Kyiv Published 1 day ago
Burnham to hand long-range missile blueprints to Zelensky as he visits Kyiv
The weapons are not new â they were developed in the 1990s - and they are expensive â at around Â£1m a piece.
They also rely on complex global supply chains and have been built in peacetime at relatively low rates â in the hundreds, not the thousands.
Even with the blueprints, Ukraine may find it hard to source components. It could take months, possibly years to make the cruise missile themselves.
Copying Western weapons production in peacetime is, in fact, no way to win a war. Even Nato nations now realise that.
Britain and many of its allies have tended to produce small quantities of highly advanced, expensive missiles which would quickly run out in any protracted conflict.
In 2021, the former head of the US Army in Europe, Gen Ben Hodges, said that in a Nato wargame the UK military ran out of key weapons within a matter of days.
Proof of the recent change in mindset is the UK military is no longer buying Storm Shadow missiles for itself.
Instead, under Project Brakestop, it is developing its own long-range cruise missiles, free of foreign components, and less than half the price of a Storm Shadow.
Project Brakestop is also being done at break-neck speed. The UK hopes to have a new cruise missile ready by the end of the year. It is promising to supply the new weapon to Ukraine.
It is Ukraine which has shown the world how to produce relatively cheap, mass produced weapons, necessary for a long, protracted conflict.

Douglas Barrie, Senior Fellow for Military Aerospace at the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) told the BBC: "The decision to share UK classified information on the MBDA SCALP missiles with Ukraine, as France and Ukraine work toward local assembly lines in Ukraine, is notable. Any impact, however, will in part depend on how quickly Ukrainian assembled SCALP cruise missiles can be introduced into service.

"Given that Ukraine has already operated both Storm Shadow and SCALP, familiarity with the missile may help speed the overall process, but this will also be dependent on the extent and pace at which local assembly can be established."
At the start of the war its armed forces relied on old Cold War-era Soviet weaponry.
A slow supply of Western weapons helped it adapt. But now Ukraine produces 70% of its own weapons.

Key has been its rapid development of drone technology â from small First Person View (FPV) one-way attack drones for the front line, to larger long-range drones capable of striking deep into Russian territory, further than Storm Shadows can strike.
Kyiv is on track to build 10 million drones by the end of this year. And they can do it cheaper than the West, by using mass-produced Chinese parts.
Nato allies' equivalent drones can be twice as expensive as they try to shun Chinese components.
However, there are still weapons that Ukraine needs and struggles to produce on its own. From fast fighter jets to the most urgent example, interceptors to take down Russian ballistic missiles

The most effective weapon to do that, by far, is the US-made Patriot interceptor. Ukraine has all but run out of them and Russian ballistic missiles now make it through Ukrainian air defences with ease.
America's war in Iran has meant they're in even shorter supply.

They're also expensive â at around Â£3m a missile â and production rates have been slow. The US is planning to double production rates from around 600 Patriot missiles per annum to 2,000, but that will take several years.
President Donald Trump signalled last month that he would be willing to share Patriot technology with Ukraine, but has since rowed back .

Even if he had given approval, it would have taken a while for Ukraine to make Patriots themselves - some estimate at least a year. Ukraine would also be relying on the same sophisticated components that are in high demand across the globe.
Ukraine has embarked on a programme to develop its own interceptor missiles with European support â known as Project Freya.
But there are huge technological challenges in building a high-speed missile to take down another missile travelling at thousands of miles per hour. It is expensive and often time consuming.
Ukraine's military and its weapons manufacturers have shown themselves to be fast learners.
One of its own companies, Fire Point, is developing its own ballistic missiles which it hopes will be ready to fire in anger next year.
But Russia has already ramped up its own ballistic missile production, to around 100 a month.
Developing sophisticated weapons is expensive and cannot be done quickly. Ukraine is short of both time and money.

So, the move to hand missile blueprints to Ukraine will be welcome, but it is not an immediate fix for Ukraine's most pressing problems, and it wwill not dramatically alter Kyiv's ability to strike Russia in new ways.

articles.title: Lockerbie bombing trial postponed days before it was due to start
articles.summary: The trial of a Libyan man is delayed for a third time, after new evidence on the 37-year-old case came to light three days ago.
articles.body:
The trial of a Libyan man over the Lockerbie bombing has been postponed for a third time, after new evidence on the 37-year-old case came to light three days ago.

Jury selection was due to get under way in Washington DC on Wednesday but the BBC understands a new start date has been set for January next year.

Lawyers acting for Abu Agila Mas'ud Kheir Al-Marimi said "newly discovered evidence" previously unknown to the defence and prosecutors from the US government emerged on Friday 21 August.

Al-Marimi has denied building the bomb that destroyed Pan Am Flight 103 on 21 December 1988, killing 270 people.

His lawyers told the court: "Constitutional and ethical obligations require the defence to investigate this development."

They said they met Al-Marimi on Sunday and he agreed that they should ask for the postponement.

The trial judge, Dabney Friedrich, has agreed that the start date should be set aside, underlining the potential importance of the new evidence.

She would have been extremely reluctant to allow an 11th hour postponement after months of preparation and marathon pre-trial legal battles.

For the relatives of those who died and Al-Marimi himself, this latest delay means a verdict might not come until next spring.

It is yet another stunning development in a saga that has witnessed countless twists and turns over nearly four decades.

Pan Am 103 was flying from Heathrow to New York when the bomb exploded in its forward hold, breaking the plane apart at 31,000 feet.

All 259 passengers and crew on board were killed. Another 11 people died in Lockerbie when the wreckage fell on their homes.

Of the victims, 190 were American and 43 from the UK.

Nearly four decades later, the bombing remains the worst terror attack and mass murder in British history.

Al-Marimi has been in US custody since 2022 and was originally due to stand trial in May 2025.

That date was set aside following a joint request from the prosecution and defence, who cited the complexity of the case and Al-Marimi's ill health.

The trial was pencilled in for April this year but was called off again, after the defence asked for more time to prepare.

The Lockerbie bombing has been the subject of a joint Scottish-US investigation since December 1988.

Prosecutors from the Crown Office and detectives from Police Scotland were due to travel to Washington to attend the case, and Scottish witnesses were expected to be among the first to give evidence at the trial.

Laura Buchan, head of the Lockerbie investigation team at the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service said: "I recognise that this adjournment will be disappointing for the families and for those who have followed this case over many years.

"As the matter remains before the court, it would not be appropriate to comment on the reasons for the adjournment.

"Although these proceedings are being led by the United States authorities, Scottish prosecutors and police officers remain fully committed to supporting the pursuit of justice."

Campaigner Kara Weipz, who is president of the Victims of Pan Am Flight 103 group, said she was "floored" when she received the news that the trial had been postponed.

She told the BBC's Radio Scotland Breakfast programme that she would pray that older relatives of victims would "remain healthy" so they can see the trial eventually take place.

She said: "It's always been my goal for as many family members to be able to witness this trial as possible and to gain more of the truth.

"If that's what this evidence brings, that's what the families have been fighting for for almost four decades - we want the truth, we want to know what happened - and if that's what this brings then this time will be worth it."

Dr Jim Swire, who has campaigned for justice since his daughter, Flora, was killed in the bombing, said he believed the delay in the trial could be beneficial if it meant more care would be taken over evidence.

He said: "For many years, we've been after only one thing, and that is the truth.

"If each delay allows the court to assemble more of the true evidence, I am all in favour of it.

"The judge seems to have stuck her oar in and insisted on further care being taken about the assembly of evidence, and if so, that is good news."

A grandfather in his 70s, Al-Marimi has been accused of carrying out the attack along with two Libyans who faced a Scottish court in May 2000.

Three judges heard the case at Camp Zeist, a former US air force base in the Netherlands.

After eight months, they ruled the atrocity was an act of state sponsored terrorism carried out by members of the Libyan intelligence service.

The judges convicted one of the Libyans, Abdulbasset Al-Megrahi, of mass murder and jailed him for life.

He died from cancer in 2012, after being freed on compassionate grounds by the Scottish government.

The Scottish Criminal Cases Review Commission twice referred Megrahi's case to the appeal court but the conviction was upheld .

The second Libyan, Al Amin Khalifah Fhimah was acquitted and returned home to a hero's welcome in Tripoli.

The US government says Al-Marimi admitted bombing the plane along with Megrahi and Fhimah when he was questioned in a Libyan detention facility in 2012.

The alleged confession was handed to Scottish investigators in 2017 and is now central to the prosecution case.

Al-Marimi has claimed the confession is false and was made under duress, but judge Friedrich ruled it can be admitted as evidence at the trial.

articles.title: Bundelkhand: Caste divides make scorching summers harder in a parched corner of India
articles.summary: Rising heat and water scarcity are deepening old caste inequalities in Bundelkhand region, activists say.
articles.body:
A couple of months ago, just after sunrise, 40-year-old Mamta began the first of as many as 10 journeys she would make that day.

Carrying three empty plastic buckets, she walked a few hundred metres to the nearest handpump in her village in Jalaun district, in the drought-prone Bundelkhand region of northern India. Temperatures in parts of the region were soaring above 40C.

The taps installed under a government drinking water scheme had been dry for two years, she said, leaving most of the village's 1,000 residents dependent on a handful of handpumps.

Mamta said collecting enough water for her 11-member family and their livestock took hours. But the heat was not her only obstacle.

Mamta belongs to the Valmiki community, part of the Dalits - groups once regarded as "untouchable" under India's centuries-old caste hierarchy and which continue to face widespread discrimination.

She said she waited until members of the village's dominant castes finished using the handpump before approaching it.

"If they are standing there, we cannot fill water. We have to wait until they leave," she said.

Afterwards, she said, some upper-caste residents poured water over the pump to "cleanse" it.

Bundelkhand, a semi-arid region that spans several districts in the states of Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh, is notoriously drought-prone. It faced several major droughts between 2002 and 2016, making it almost a symbol for water scarcity in a country where several regions face similar hardships.

The rocky terrain of the Bundelkhand plateau means it can store little groundwater. Erratic rainfall and hotter temperatures have also made access to water unpredictable despite several government and community-led conservation efforts.

A study of more than a century of weather records found temperatures had risen across almost the entire region, and in recent summers, parts of Bundelkhand have neared 48C.

Residents and researchers say worsening heat and water stress are putting new pressure on an old divide.

As more families compete for scarce shared water, Dalits who have long faced barriers in accessing it are encountering those inequalities more often.

"Conflict over water is not new," said Mitashi Singh of the Centre for Science and Environment.

"What is changing is the role hotter summers are playing in making water scarcer and intensifying tensions that already existed."

Local officials reject claims that the region faces water shortages or caste discrimination at public water sources.

Dominant-caste residents interviewed by the BBC also denied discriminating against others, although they acknowledged growing pressure on water supplies.

Ram Gopal Singh, who is in his 50s, pointed to several abandoned village wells.

"These wells have been dry for almost 20 years," he said. Other sources had dried up or become polluted, while unreliable tap connections had pushed more families towards handpumps.

Everyone tried to collect water in the cooler morning hours, he said, leading to arguments over turns and how much each family could take.

"But there is no caste-based dispute at these handpumps," he insisted.

Dalit residents interviewed by the BBC described something different.

There is no formal queue at the pumps, they said. Instead, families try to collect water at different times to avoid confrontations.

Mamta said she usually went very early in the morning or late in the afternoon.

"The fear of being targeted stays with me throughout," she said.

About 50km away in Shahjahanpur, Shiv described a similar experience.

He said members of his community would not approach the handpump while dominant-caste families were using it.

"No matter how hot it is, even if we have to wait for hours for one bucket of drinking water, we wait because we do not have a choice," he said.

In summer, when his family needed more water, those waiting periods became more frequent.

"Even if my parents are thirsty, we sometimes wait for hours before we can drink."

Three years ago, Shiv's mother Parmi Devi said she was assaulted after an argument with a member of a dominant caste at a village handpump.

"I was thrashed and beaten up and thrown on the ground three times," she alleged.

"It was not just about water. It was because of our caste."

Devi filed a police complaint alleging assault. No arrests have been made yet.

Such disputes have surfaced repeatedly in complaints documented by the Dalit Dignity and Justice Centre (DDJC), a non-profit organisation in Uttar Pradesh.

The group said police registered 113 cases under India's law against caste-based atrocities in the area in 2025.

Kuldeep Singh Baudh of DDJC told BBC Hindi a majority of the complaints it tracked during the hottest months of May and June involved water, though the organisation has not published a detailed breakdown.

"To truly understand [the heat's] impact, you have to see it from the perspective of the communities that are the most excluded," he said.

The office of District Magistrate Rajesh Kumar Pandey rejected the allegations.

"There is not even one instance wherein caste-based discrimination is being practised when it comes to access to water in the region," it said in a statement.

The statement also disputed claims of water shortages, pointing to the federal government's Jal Jeevan Mission, which aims to provide piped drinking water to every rural household, and other local efforts to restore ponds and recharge groundwater.

There have also been wider efforts to tackle Bundelkhand's water crisis. Traditional water bodies, including ponds and check dams, have been revived across the region, while women-led groups known as Jal Sahelis work in villages to monitor supplies and promote water conservation.

Mukul Sharma, a researcher on caste and environmental politics, said increasing water supplies was only part of the solution.

Climate change is "not the origin of these injustices, but a threat multiplier", he added.

More water alone will not solve the problem if caste still shapes who gets to use it, Sharma said.

That morning in May, Mamta waited beside the handpump as other families filled their buckets, three empty plastic containers at her feet.

In cooler months, she said, she made the journey only a few times a day. In summer, it could be eight or 10, each trip determined partly by who was already at the pump.

When her turn came, she filled her buckets and carried them home. Later that day, she would return.

articles.title: Ajit Dovalâs China visit: NSA, Chinese VP Han Zheng discuss border peace, bilateral ties
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: National security advisor Ajit Doval on Tuesday met Chinese vice president Han Zheng in Beijing, with the two sides discussing ways to main.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: National security advisor Ajit Doval on Tuesday met Chinese vice president Han Zheng in Beijing, with the two sides discussing ways to maintain peace and tranquillity along the border and further strengthen India-China relations across economic, political and multilateral platforms.The meeting came ahead of the 25th round of special representatives talks on the India-China boundary question between Doval and Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi later on Tuesday.Sharing details of the meeting, the Embassy of India in China said, "On 25 August, NSA and Special Representative on the India-China Boundary Question, Ajit Doval called on Han Zheng, Vice President of the People's Republic of China."The embassy said Doval and Han discussed ways to strengthen peace and tranquillity in the border areas and further improve bilateral ties "across economic, political and multilateral fora", in line with the consensus reached by the leaders of the two countries.Doval arrived in Beijing on Monday for a two-day visit to participate in the Special Representatives talks with Wang Yi, who is also China's Foreign Minister.The talks are expected to focus on the boundary question, along with bilateral, regional and international issues.The Chinese Foreign Ministry has described the Special Representatives mechanism as the "main channel" for negotiations between the two countries on the boundary question and an important platform for communication on issues of mutual interest.The mechanism was established in 2003 to address the India-China boundary dispute, which stretches across roughly 3,488 km.The 24th round of talks was held in August last year, when the two sides held what Beijing described as candid and in-depth discussions and reached several common understandings.The upcoming round assumes significance as India and China seek to stabilise ties following years of tensions along the Line of Actual Control.The discussions come amid efforts by New Delhi and Beijing to gradually improve bilateral relations after the 2020 Galwan Valley clash and the prolonged military stand-off in eastern Ladakh severely strained ties.Doval and Wang had also met in June in New Delhi on the sidelines of the BRICS National Security Advisers' meeting. The Ministry of External Affairs had described those discussions as "constructive and forward-looking".MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal had said, "The two sides reviewed recent developments in bilateral relations and noted progress towards gradual normalisation. NSA underlined that stable, predictable and constructive bilateral relations contribute to building trust and better understanding between the two sides. The discussions were constructive and forward-looking."The latest talks also come amid efforts by the two countries to build on a series of high-level engagements between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping.The leaders had welcomed positive momentum and steady progress in bilateral relations during their meeting on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Tianjin last year, after their previous meeting in Kazan in October 2024.They had reaffirmed that India and China are development partners rather than rivals and that differences should not be allowed to become disputes."A stable relationship and cooperation between India and China and their 2.8 billion peoples on the basis of mutual respect, mutual interest and mutual sensitivity are necessary for the growth and development of the two countries, as well as for a multipolar world and a multi-polar Asia befitting the trends of the 21st century," the MEA had said after the leaders' meeting.Despite the gradual improvement in ties, differences over the boundary and Arunachal Pradesh remain sensitive issues between New Delhi and Beijing.Both Doval and Wang are designated Special Representatives for the boundary talks mechanism. While the process has not resolved the long-running border dispute, officials on both sides continue to regard it as an important channel for managing tensions and maintaining communication.The talks also come ahead of Xi's expected visit to New Delhi for the BRICS summit on September 12-13, which could provide an opportunity for another meeting between Xi and PM Modi and further discussions on the bilateral relationship.Get the latest India News and Live updates. tranquillity in the border areas and further improve bilateral ties "across economic, political and multilateral fora", in line with the consensus reached by the leaders of the two countries.Doval arrived in Beijing on Monday for a two-day visit to participate in the Special Representatives talks with Wang Yi, who is also China's Foreign Minister.The talks are expected to focus on the boundary question, along with bilateral, regional and international issues.The Chinese Foreign Ministry has described the Special Representatives mechanism as the "main channel" for negotiations between the two countries on the boundary question and an important platform for communication on issues of mutual interest.The mechanism was established in 2003 to address the India-China boundary dispute, which stretches across roughly 3,488 km.The 24th round of talks was held in August last year, when the two sides held what Beijing described as candid and in-depth discussions and reached several common understandings.The upcoming round assumes significance as India and China seek to stabilise ties following years of tensions along the Line of Actual Control.The discussions come amid efforts by New Delhi and Beijing to gradually improve bilateral relations after the 2020 Galwan Valley clash and the prolonged military stand-off in eastern Ladakh severely strained ties.Doval and Wang had also met in June in New Delhi on the sidelines of the BRICS National Security Advisers' meeting. The Ministry of External Affairs had described those discussions as "constructive and forward-looking".MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal had said, "The two sides reviewed recent developments in bilateral relations and noted progress towards gradual normalisation. NSA underlined that stable, predictable and constructive bilateral relations contribute to building trust and better understanding between the two sides. The discussions were constructive and forward-looking."The latest talks also come amid efforts by the two countries to build on a series of high-level engagements between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping.The leaders had welcomed positive momentum and steady progress in bilateral relations during their meeting on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Tianjin last year, after their previous meeting in Kazan in October 2024.They had reaffirmed that India and China are development partners rather than rivals and that differences should not be allowed to become disputes."A stable relationship and cooperation between India and China and their 2.8 billion peoples on the basis of mutual respect, mutual interest and mutual sensitivity are necessary for the growth and development of the two countries, as well as for a multipolar world and a multi-polar Asia befitting the trends of the 21st century," the MEA had said after the leaders' meeting.Despite the gradual improvement in ties, differences over the boundary and Arunachal Pradesh remain sensitive issues between New Delhi and Beijing.Both Doval and Wang are designated Special Representatives for the boundary talks mechanism. While the process has not resolved the long-running border dispute, officials on both sides continue to regard it as an important channel for managing tensions and maintaining communication.The talks also come ahead of Xi's expected visit to New Delhi for the BRICS summit on September 12-13, which could provide an opportunity for another meeting between Xi and PM Modi and further discussions on the bilateral relationship.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Myanmar's human rights crisis has hit new low': UN flags atrocities against Rohingya
articles.summary: South Asia News: The human rights situation in Myanmar has reached a new low, with widespread atrocities against the Rohingya minority and a rapidly expanding illicit .
articles.body: The human rights situation in Myanmar has reached a new low, with widespread atrocities against the Rohingya minority and a rapidly expanding illicit economy further deepening the suffering of civilians, the United Nations said on Tuesday.According to a report by the UN human rights office covering the period from June 2025 to May 2026, unrelenting conflict, military violence and a growing âconflict economyâ have exposed millions of civilians to severe hardship.Both the Myanmar military and the Arakan Army, which controls large parts of Rakhine State, have been accused of systemic abuses against Rohingya communities. These include killings, torture, forced labour, forced recruitment, arbitrary detention, sexual violence and forced displacement.Nearly nine years after the military crackdown that triggered the mass exodus of Rohingya in 2017, the community continues to face persecution and displacement. The situation has deteriorated further since the military coup in February 2021 that ousted Aung San Suu Kyi and plunged the country into a prolonged civil war.The military-backed electoral process held earlier this year paved the way for junta leader Min Aung Hlaing to become president, while the military continued to consolidate its grip over the country.The UN said the military had continued to use airstrikes, arson and restrictions on humanitarian assistance to terrorise civilians and maintain control. At least 8,075 civilians, including 1,774 women and 1,074 children, have been killed since the 2021 coup, according to UN figures. The actual toll is believed to be significantly higher.Myanmarâs military has denied deliberately targeting civilians, saying its airstrikes were limited to military targets and were carried out in response to armed groups seizing towns and villages. It has also described several of the groups fighting it as terrorist organisations.The conflict has also triggered a massive humanitarian crisis. The number of internally displaced people has risen to about 3.6 million, while an estimated 12.4 million people are facing acute food insecurity. Among those affected are hundreds of thousands of women and children suffering from acute malnutrition.Rohingya caught between two armed forcesThe UN has accused the Arakan Army of carrying out serious abuses against Rohingya communities in northern Rakhine, including arbitrary arrests, torture, sexual abuse and forced labour.The group has also been accused of seizing Rohingya land and preventing displaced people from returning to their homes, while allowing non-Rohingya communities to settle on some confiscated properties.Satellite imagery reviewed by the UN indicates that around 2,000 acres of land have been seized. Witness accounts also describe children as young as six being subjected to forced labour.Former detainees have reported torture in custody, with some inmates allegedly dying as a result of their treatment.The abuses have left the Rohingya trapped between competing armed forces, with neither the military nor the Arakan Army providing meaningful protection from persecution and violence.Myanmarâs hidden mining economyThe conflict has also created a parallel economy that is helping finance armed groups while devastating local communities and the environment.The UN report highlights the rapid expansion of illegal rare-earth mining in Kachin and Shan states, where the collapse of the rule of law has allowed illicit industries to flourish.In Kachin, at least 302 new mining sites have emerged since the 2021 coup. In Shan State, the number of sites has increased from just 12 before the coup to 85.The rare-earth trade reached an estimated peak value of $1.4 billion in 2023, with much of the output flowing into Chinaâs market, according to the UN.But the economic gains have come at a devastating environmental and human cost.Toxic chemicals released during mining have contaminated waterways and farmland, contributing to chronic illnesses and reported miscarriages among communities living near mining areas.The pollution is also crossing national borders. Contaminated water has reached rivers flowing into Thailand, where testing has detected elevated levels of arsenic, lead, mercury and manganese.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘No downside’: Warren Buffett trusts 2 key assets for his grandkids — and says the income will likely jump for decades
articles.summary: Buffett’s decades-old bets reveal a simple formula: Buy productive assets at the right price, then let their income and value compound over time.
articles.body:
Moneywise and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue through links in the content below.

Warren Buffett is best known as one of the greatest stock market investors of all time.

But some of the investments he has spoken most glowingly about aren't stocks at all.

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

JPMorgan sees gold hitting $5,000/oz by Q4 — and savvy investors are protecting their wealth with a tax-advantaged Gold IRA. Get your free guide from Priority Gold

The tax breaks in Trump's 'big beautiful bill' expire after 2028. Here are 4 moves to make before the window closes

In a letter to Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE: BRK.B) shareholders, Buffett reflected on two personal investments he had made decades earlier — both far outside his usual world of publicly traded companies.

While not as famous as Berkshire's stock holdings, Buffett has expressed unwavering confidence in these investments.

"The two investments will be solid and satisfactory holdings for my lifetime and, subsequently, for my children and grandchildren," he wrote (1).

He also projected that the income from the two investments "will probably increase in the decades to come."

The answer reveals a lot about how the legendary investor thinks about building wealth that can last for generations.

The first opportunity appeared in 1986, after a bubble in asset prices had burst in the Midwest.

Buffett paid $280,000 for a 400-acre property about 50 miles north of Omaha — considerably less than the amount a failed bank had previously lent against it.

The Oracle of Omaha admitted that he "knew nothing" about operating a farm. But his son had a passion for farming, and Buffett was able to learn about the farm's production of corn and soybeans and its operating expenses.

Buffett then calculated that the normalized return from the farm would be 10%. He also believed that productivity would likely improve over time and that crop prices would increase. He highlighted that "both expectations proved out."

It didn't seem to be a hard decision to make, as he remarked, "I needed no unusual knowledge or intelligence to conclude that the investment had no downside and potentially had substantial upside."

That confidence paid off. Buffett noted that the farm had tripled its earnings by 2014 and was worth five times more than what he paid.

articles.title: Fortescue defended keeping an executive at work during a harassment investigation; days later it reversed course and suspended the employee
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Fortescue is facing renewed scrutiny over workplace conduct as an external investigation into allegations involving a senior executive runs alongside .
articles.body: Fortescue is facing renewed scrutiny over workplace conduct as an external investigation into allegations involving a senior executive runs alongside separate legal action brought by former employees. The mining company has confirmed that law firm MinterEllison is examining the allegations, while the executive remains employed as the inquiry continues. At the same time, a class action filed in July alleges broader workplace misconduct, including sexual harassment. The case follows similar proceedings involving BHP and Rio Tinto, putting workplace culture across some of Australia's biggest mining companies under growing attention.Fortescue's own annual figures add another layer to the story, with reported psychosocial breaches falling during the latest financial year. But those numbers cover a wider range of workplace concerns and cannot be treated as a direct measure of sexual misconduct. The separate investigations, court cases and internal reporting figures show how difficult it can be to assess workplace conduct through any single set of numbers.Fortescue has hired MinterEllison to investigate allegations against an unnamed senior executiveFortescue confirmed that MinterEllison had been engaged to examine allegations concerning the unnamed senior executive. The company has also sought outside legal and governance advice about how the matter should be handled while the inquiry continues.Gus Pichot, Fortescue's energy chief, said during an earnings call that the company believed it was following the appropriate process. The executive remains employed while the investigation is taking place.That arrangement means the allegations have not yet been resolved. The investigation is intended to establish what happened and whether any workplace rules or standards were breached.The allegations were first reported by the Australian Financial Review earlier in August. Fortescue has not publicly identified the executive involved.98 psychosocial breaches, with 11 dismissals over misconduct recordedThe investigation comes alongside Fortescue's annual disclosure of workplace conduct figures. The miner recorded 98 psychosocial breaches during the latest financial year, a 20% fall from the previous year.The category covers a range of workplace concerns rather than sexual harassment alone. It includes matters such as ethical issues and other incidents that can affect employees' psychological wellbeing.Fortescue said 11 employees had been dismissed for breaches of its code of conduct involving discrimination and sexual harassment. Its internal findings included 13 cases of inappropriate sexual contact, 10 cases of sexual harassment and one case classified as sexual assault.âSexual harassment, unlawful discrimination and any behavior that makes people feel unsafe have no place at Fortescue.âAs reported by Australian Financial Review (AFR), the company employs 16,154 people. Those figures provide a broader picture than the investigation involving the senior executive. They cover cases dealt with across the organisation during the financial year and do not indicate the outcome of the current inquiry.Mining's long-running workplace problemSexual harassment has remained a difficult issue for Australia's resources industry, particularly in Western Australia, where mining is a major employer and workplace culture at remote sites has faced scrutiny for years.A state inquiry into sexual harassment in the resources sector began in 2021. Its findings brought greater attention to complaints about inappropriate behaviour and the difficulties workers can face when reporting misconduct in workplaces where power structures can be pronounced.The issue has not been confined to Fortescue. BHP, the world's largest mining company by market value, reported 380 sexual harassment complaints in its latest financial year, an 11% reduction from the previous year. It also said 109 employees had been dismissed for sexual harassment and 22 for racial harassment.BHP's workforce, including contractors, numbers more than 84,000 globally, so its figures cover a much larger employee base than Fortescue's.Rio Tinto sees Care Hub reports climb, highlighting the limits of comparisonsReportedly, Rio Tinto has reported a different trend in the number of matters reaching its employee support system. The miner recorded 702 incidents through its Care Hub during 2025, a 24% increase from the previous year. The service deals with a broad range of harmful or disrespectful workplace behaviour, including harassment, rather than focusing solely on sexual misconduct.The figures from the three mining companies cannot be read as a direct league table. Their reporting systems, definitions and workforce sizes differ, and an increase in reports can reflect changes in reporting behaviour as well as changes in the underlying level of misconduct.A fall in complaints does not necessarily mean every form of harmful behaviour has declined, just as a rise can sometimes indicate that employees have become more willing or able to report what they experience.Western Australia has seen a fall in reported casesAs reported by Reuters, WorkSafe Western Australia also points to a reduction in incidents reported to the state regulator. WorkSafe recorded 28 incidents involving sexual assault and harassment during the first six months of 2026. That compares with 113 incidents across the whole of 2025 and 421 in 2022.The regulator linked the decline to the work of a specialist team established after the state inquiry. The team has expanded the regulator's capacity to respond to reports involving sexual harassment and assault.The figures cover reports received by the regulator and should not be taken as a measure of every incident occurring across the state's workplaces. Many cases may never reach a regulator.Fortescue faces legal action as its senior executive misconduct probe continuesFortescue is also facing legal action over alleged workplace misconduct. A class action filed in July alleges misconduct including sexual harassment and sex discrimination. The potential damages have not yet been specified.The case was brought by law firm JGA Saddler, which has also filed class actions against BHP and Rio Tinto over alleged workplace misconduct. Those proceedings, launched in late 2024, remain before the courts. The legal cases and Fortescue's internal figures are separate from the investigation now being conducted by MinterEllison. The external inquiry concerns allegations against a particular senior executive, while the class action addresses broader claims about workplace conduct.For Fortescue, the immediate issue is therefore being handled on two fronts: an investigation into allegations involving a senior figure and continuing legal scrutiny over wider workplace practices.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Nigeria kidnappings: President Bola Tinubu orders manhunt after victim video uploaded
articles.summary: The footage shows dozens of men, women and children sitting in a forest.
articles.body:
Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu has ordered a manhunt for armed kidnappers who launched deadly attacks on four villages in a remote part of Niger state last Friday.

Local residents told the BBC several mosques were simultaneously targeted during prayers. A local youth leader says as many as 500 people may have been abducted, though this has not been verified.

The president's orders came after the kidnappers posted a video on social media of what they said were those abducted last week sitting in a forest.

The authorities had previously suspected the attackers were bandits - criminal gangs involved in kidnapping and looting for ransom across parts of Nigeria.

The kidnap gangs, jihadists and separatists wreaking havoc in Nigeria Published 28 November 2025

The kidnap gangs, jihadists and separatists wreaking havoc in Nigeria

The gunmen, reportedly dressed in military-style clothing, attacked the villages of Dekara, Gidan Zana, Sabon Gida and Masaka.

Police spokesman Wasiu Abiodun told the BBC that more than 40 people were killed, but the exact number of deaths had not been confirmed.

Looking at the footage released on social media, the local youth leader, who asked not to be named, said he recognised several individuals from his community.

"I was able to identify many people. There is an elderly man in the video who is like a grandfather to us," he said. "He lives in Gidan Zana village."

He said families who had spotted relatives in the video were relieved to know they were still alive.

"At least they know where their loved ones are and hope they may be rescued, unlike those who still have no information about missing relatives," he added.

A local blogger familiar with the area told the BBC that many residents had fled their homes, seeking refuge in neighbouring states or across the border in Benin.

Some survivors are receiving hospital treatment, including people with serious injuries.

A local official also told the BBC that the attackers planted improvised explosive devices in parts of the affected communities as they led abductees into the forest. He said a teenage boy was killed when an explosive detonated as he tried to escape.

In a statement issued by presidential spokesman Bayo Onanuga, Tinubu condemned the killings and abductions and vowed that those responsible would be brought to justice.

"Those who carried out this cowardly attack on defenceless Nigerians are enemies of peace and enemies of humanity, who will not go scot-free," the statement said.

The president also expressed his condolences to the families of those killed.

The attack is the latest sign of worsening insecurity in the Borgu area, which borders Kebbi and Kwara states as well as neighbouring Benin.

Earlier this month, police said 145 people had been rescued after being abducted from four other villages in the area.

Local officials have also raised concerns about the growing presence of jihadist groups operating in parts of north-western Nigeria and along the border region, saying some fighters have recently entered communities and imposed religious restrictions on residents.

articles.title: Nearly 6-foot cobra hiding under kitchen sends India family rushing to safety
articles.summary: Frightened residents may try to trap or kill it instead of calling trained professionals.
articles.body:
A nearly six-foot cobra hiding beneath a kitchen in India sent one family rushing to safety after hissing and movement inside the home revealed a dangerous surprise.

As The Live Nagpur reported , the rescue ended without injury to either the residents or the snake, but the incident showed how quickly a wildlife encounter can become a major safety concern.

At around 2 p.m. on Aug. 11, 2026, the Songade family left their home in Gayatri Colony and alerted neighbors after tracing hissing and movement in the kitchen to a cobra concealed beneath the kitchen area, the publication said.

As neighbors gathered outside, Shubham G.R., president of Wild Animals and Nature Helping Society, was called to the scene. He captured the cobra from the kitchen and released it into the wild, according to TLN.

A venomous cobra inside a home poses a serious risk, especially in a confined indoor space. In India, these types of events crop up from time to time, and it can be alarming for locals.

While it is unclear exactly why this cobra entered the house, situations like this can be linked in part to human activity.

As homes, roads, and neighborhoods expand into or alongside wildlife habitat, animals and people are pushed into closer contact. Even common features around homes, including dark corners, stored belongings, food scraps, and rodents, can make residential spaces appealing hiding spots for snakes.

The BBC has reported that human expansion into natural spaces can increase dangerous encounters with wild animals, creating risks for both residents and animals trying to navigate altered environments.

A cobra in a kitchen can drive a family from their home and cause panic throughout a neighborhood. The situation can also turn deadly for the snake, as frightened residents may try to trap or kill it instead of calling trained professionals.

Instead of trying to deal with the cobra themselves, TLN noted the family kept away from it, alerted others, and sought help from a trained rescuer.

Wildlife rescuers say that is the right response when a snake is found indoors. People should keep their distance, make sure children and pets stay away from the area, and contact an authorized wildlife rescue team or trained snake rescuer as quickly as possible.

Reducing the chances of similar encounters can involve keeping homes and nearby areas clean, limiting places where snakes can hide, and addressing conditions that attract prey animals such as rodents.

Those steps may not eliminate the risk entirely, particularly in places close to wildlife habitat, but they can help reduce the odds of a frightening encounter inside the home.

Fortunately, in this case, the family was unharmed, and the cobra was removed safely, avoiding a much worse outcome.

articles.title: West African cyber-crime networks: Mass arrests follow Interpol crackdown
articles.summary: The operation included the arrest of 39 people in South Africa for romance and investment scams.
articles.body:
Fifty-eight people linked to organised West African cyber-crime groups have been arrested in an operation across 22 countries and six continents.

Dubbed "Operation Jackal IV", it was co-ordinated by the global policing agency Interpol, targeting those behind romance and investment scams. It also identified 263 suspects.

Interpol said it was a response to the escalating global threat posed by these criminal networks - such as the feared Nigerian Black Axe group - believed to be behind a "significant share" of cyber-enabled financial fraud.

The operation also allowed analysis of emerging trends such as how these groups use sextortion to target minors, with victims as young as 14.

The ultra-violent cult that became a global mafia Published 13 December 2021

The ultra-violent cult that became a global mafia

Operation Jackal IV - which took place between November 2025 and June 2026 - investigated how the groups laundered money and how financial fraud cyber crimes, such as cryptocurrency and email compromise fraud, were conducted.

Scams often targeted "retirees in English-speaking countries", Interpol said.

"By following illicit financial flows across borders, we are attacking the very lifeblood of organised crime and making it increasingly difficult for criminal networks to profit from their activities," Tomonobu Kaya, director of Interpol's financial crime centre, said in a statement.

"Operation Jackal IV demonstrates the power of international co-operation."

During the operation, Interpol helped with cross-border co-ordination and intelligence sharing.

It also provided support and specialised training for money-laundering investigations with the participating countries.

Interpol said many aspects of Jackal IV remained under investigation but preliminary outcomes included arrests in Argentina, Italy, Romania and South Africa.

In South Africa, seven sites linked to a syndicate involved in romance and investment scams were raided.

The policing agency was on scene in Johannesburg to support local authorities during the raids.

South African police made 39 arrests, seized $2.67m (Â£1.96m) and blocked 257 bank accounts.

As well as cyber-enabled fraud, the West African networks also participated in other serious and violent crimes, Interpol said.

Operation Jackal IV is one of multiple "Jackal" police operations that have taken place since 2022.

In 2024, Jackal III led to the arrests of 300 people linked to Black Axe and other affiliated groups.

Black Axe is a shadowy criminal network with trafficking, prostitution and killing operations around the world.

Nigeria is its main recruitment ground and many of its members are university educated and inducted during their schooling.
