articles.title: The Syrian Democratic Forces, tip of the spear in anti-jihadist fight
articles.summary: The Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, whose dissolution was announced by their leader Mazloum Abdi on Tuesday, were the Washington-backed de facto army o...
articles.body:
The Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, whose dissolution was announced by their leader Mazloum Abdi on Tuesday, were the Washington-backed de facto army of the Kurds' autonomous administration in Syria and spearheaded the battle against jihadists.

The force was Syria's most highly trained and organised for years, until Washington dropped them for the new US-friendly authorities in Damascus.

Experts say the SDF's dissolution marks the end of an era for the country's Kurds, who had long dreamt of autonomy before the 2024 fall of Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad.

The force was formed in 2015 at the instigation of the United States, impressed by the Kurdish fighters who had defeated the Islamic State group in Kobane in the north, and seeking a reliable partner in the battle against the jihadists.

The SDF then led the battle against IS, which was defeated territorially in Syria four years later.

The force amassed around 100,000 fighters at its peak, was composed of Kurds and Arabs, and controlled swathes of Syria's oil-rich north and northeast.

But following January clashes that saw the Kurds lose large chunks of territory to government troops, the two sides signed a deal to integrate Kurdish military and civilian institutions into the state.

Arabs within their ranks also defected en masse after Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa's army took control of two previously Kurdish-held provinces, Raqa and Deir Ezzor, leaving them weakened.

"Dissolving for SDF means a bitter end" for the Kurds, Mutlu Civiroglu, a Washington-based analyst and expert on the Kurds, told AFP, adding that it marked "the end of Kurdish strength in Syria".

The Kurdish force was also faced with repeated Turkish invasions between 2016 and 2019, with Ankara saying it wanted to push these fighters away from its border.

Turkey has long viewed the SDF as linked to the Kurdish militant Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), which waged a decades-long insurgency in the country.

The SDF was dominated by the People's Protection Units (YPG), a Kurdish militant group seen by Ankara as an extension of the PKK.

Following a call by its jailed leader Abdullah Ocalan, the PKK formally renounced its armed struggle against Turkey in May last year, drawing a line under four decades of violence that has claimed around 50,000 lives.

The People's Protection Units denied any links with the PKK, but it was "indeed the PKK that directs the YPG behind the scenes", Syria specialist Fabrice Balanche said before the SDF dissolution.

"The YPG was formed in 2011 by PKK veterans," including SDF chief Abdi, Syria analyst Nanar Hawach of the International Crisis Group told AFP prior to Tuesday's announcement.

The January agreement with Damascus, under which Kurdish fighters would be integrated into state structures, stipulates that the SDF commit to expelling all non-Syrian PKK leaders and members from the country.

"While limited in number, they have held significant influence in command and administrative roles," Hawach told AFP, adding their numbers are estimated in the hundreds to low thousands.

In a speech earlier in August, Abdi acknowledged that "thousands of young Kurdish men and women" supported the SDF from "other parts of Kurdistan", referring to areas of Iran, Iraq and Turkey.

He also affirmed that, "at our request and according to a practical plan, those forces withdrew from here, and we can say that a new phase has begun in this region."

The SDF's integration into the state is a major victory for Sharaa, who has been trying to cement control over all of Syria since Assad's ousting.

articles.title: UN chief condemns Haiti gang attack that killed at least 47
articles.summary: UN Secretary General António Guterres has condemned a gang attack in Haiti that killed at least 47 people, including 22 who were reportedly executed at a chu...
articles.body:
UN Secretary General António Guterres has condemned a gang attack in Haiti that killed at least 47 people, including 22 who were reportedly executed at a church compound where they had sought shelter.

The attack took place at the weekend in Kenscoff, a community on the outskirts of the capital Port-au-Prince.

"The relentless gang attacks on communities and the loss of lives underscore the alarming security conditions in Haiti and reinforce the urgent need to intensify Haitian and international security efforts to counter gangs," Guterres' spokesman, Stéphane Dujarric, said in a statement on Tuesday.

Guterres also reiterated his call for Haitian authorities to "ensure that those responsible for such attacks are held accountable," including through specialized judicial units recently established with international support to investigate mass crimes.

According to the UN Integrated Office in Haiti (BINUH), more than 50 people were also abducted and 22 injured in Sunday night's attack on Kenscoff, around 10 kilometres south of Port-au-Prince.

The attackers targeted the centre of the community, setting numerous homes on fire and storming a church compound where displaced people had sought shelter, broadcaster Radio Télé Galaxie reported.

The UN's Dujarric said it was believed that 22 of the victims were killed at the church complex.

Police eventually managed to push back the attackers and regain control of the area.

Haiti's transitional government confirmed the attack but did not provide a death toll. It described the violence as a "heinous criminal attack," placed security forces on the highest level of alert and deployed reinforcements.

Criminal gangs have been trying for years to seize control of Kenscoff because of the mountainous community's strategic location, which allows control over key road connections.

Kenscoff is also close to Pétion-Ville, a comparatively affluent suburb of the capital that is home to numerous institutions, embassies and banks.

The community lies at an altitude of around 2,000 metres and, thanks to its cooler climate, is considered a relatively desirable residential area in the Caribbean country, which has been plagued by poverty and violence.

Haiti has been without a president since the assassination of Jovenel Moïse in July 2021, while an already precarious security situation has spiralled out of control.

Violent gangs control more than 80% of Port-au-Prince and have increasingly expanded into other communities, terrorizing residents, raping women and recruiting children.

According to UN figures, armed gangs killed 2,300 people in Haiti in the first five months of this year alone. More than 1,100 others were injured and almost 100 abducted.

Haiti, the poorest country in the Americas, is due to hold elections on December 13, its first since 2016.

articles.title: Govt seeks 2 years to frame creamy layer criteria for PSU, private staff kids
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Seeking two years to frame creamy layer criteria for OBCs, Centre Tuesday requested Supreme Court for an early hearing on its application a.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Seeking two years to frame creamy layer criteria for OBCs, Centre Tuesday requested Supreme Court for an early hearing on its application against retrospective implementation of SCâs March 11 judgement, which disallowed this classification of OBC candidates based on the salaries of parents employed in PSUs or the private sector.Solicitor general Tushar Mehta requested a bench led by CJI Surya Kant to list the application seeking certain clarifications on the March 11 judgement in the Rohit Nathan case. This was opposed by advocate Varun Thakur, who said the law was settled by SC.The SG said Centre was not seeking review or modification of the judgement but wanted to apprise the court of field-level difficulties in retrospective implementation. The SG said this would require changing the status of older batches of creamy layer OBC candidates to non-creamy and warrant change in cadre, post and service in civil services. articles.title: NMC pushes old doctors to re-register, but canât net new ones
articles.summary: India News: National Medical Commission (NMC) is seeking to re-register around 11 lakh doctors to create an updated national medical registry, yet it has failed t.
articles.body: National Medical Commission (NMC) is seeking to re-register around 11 lakh doctors to create an updated national medical registry, yet it has failed to register even fresh entrants to the profession despite many state registries sharing records every year, reports Rema Nagarajan.Based on MBBS seats and pass rates, at least 68,000 new doctors should have registered to practice, but only 44,400 entries were recorded in 2025 with at least 24,000 graduates missing in Indian Medical Register. The gap points to potential failure of NMC to sync state and national registries, as required under NMC Act.NMC pushes old docs to re-register, but canât net new onesThe National Medical Commission (NMC) is pushing a regulation to make about 11 lakh doctors re-register to create an updated national medical registry, but it has failed to even register fresh entrants to the profession despite many state registries sending it new entries every year.With over 91,000 MBBS seats available in 2020-21, even with an estimated 75-90% pass percentage, at least 68,000 MBBS graduates should have registered to practice in 2025. Yet the Indian Medical Register shows just over 44,400 entries. That means at least 24,000 of those who graduated just last year are missing from the registry.If thousands of foreign medical graduates who register each year are included, the number of freshly minted doctors missing from the registry would be even more. For instance, in 2023, over 10,000 foreign medical graduates passed the qualifying exam, after which they have to complete a mandatory one-year internship before receiving permanent registration that would make them eligible to practice in India. So, most of these 10,000 would have registered in 2025. Thus, the total number of doctors registering in 2025 would be roughly 80,000, but just over half the number (55%) have been added to the registry.Most of the doctors would have registered with state medical councils. However, new entries in state medical council registries are not being reflected in the national registry as the NMC is yet to synchronise all state registries with the national registry. The NMC Act, 2019, had mandated such synchronisation. It is yet to happen, almost six years after the NMC was constituted in Sept 2020. Neither is NMC adding the new entries that many state councils send every year.Take Assam Medical Council, for instance. It is a state with only govt medical colleges. In the national registry, there are a total of 25,722 registrations from the state council. It shows only one entry for 2025, zero for 2024 and 2023, 106 entries for 2022 and 353 in 2021. The website shows 890 registered in 2024. There were over 720 seats in Assam in 2015 and 1,000 seats in 2020. How is NMC accepting zero entries in 2023 and 2024, or only 106 in 2022?Similarly, NMCâs registry has a total of 67,142 entries from Kerala with just seven entries in 2025 and 17 in 2024. In 2014, Kerala had 3,650 MBBS seats, which increased to 4,500 by 2020. âWe are sending details every year... In the name of a new updated NMR, they are not updating the existing one,â said KSMC chief Dr Harikumaran Nair.If the NMC were to register only those who became doctors in the last five years, including foreign medical graduates, it would have had an updated registry of over 3.5 lakh doctors (32%) of the estimated 11 lakh who are said to be available.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Cyclosporiasis cases in US climb to 17,180, CDC says
articles.summary: Aug 25 () - The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Tuesday reported 17,180 confirmed ‌cases of cyclosporiasis in the United States, ‌an increase o...
articles.body:
Aug 25 (Reuters) - The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Tuesday reported 17,180 confirmed ‌cases of cyclosporiasis in the United States, ‌an increase of 1,464 cases from a week ago.

• The CDC said it has received reports of 17,180 confirmed cases across 48 states plus the District of Columbia, with 922 hospitalizations and two deaths ‌as of August 24. ⁠At least 11,844 additional cases may require further investigation and analysis, CDC said.

• ⁠The data include the cases reported in the ongoing multistate outbreak linked to recalled iceberg lettuce, CDC ​said, adding ​that it is investigating ​multiple clusters of cyclosporiasis.

• ‌CDC and FDA are investigating at least six other clusters for which sources have not yet been confirmed, CDC said.

• Michigan, the hardest-hit state, logged a slow 3% rise to 14,277 last week, hinting ‌the outbreak may be easing.

• ​The cyclosporiasis outbreak is one ​of the largest foodborne ​illness events in recent U.S. history. ‌The illness is caused by ​the cyclospora ​parasite, which can lead to diarrhea, nausea and other gastrointestinal symptoms.

• The outbreak has shaken U.S. ​consumers nationwide, causing ‌many to forgo eating fresh produce or ​dining in restaurants.

(Reporting by Christy Santhosh in Bengaluru; ​Editing by Vijay Kishore)

articles.title: Ram Temple donation âscamâ whistleblower gets protection from arrest
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Tuesday granted interim protection from arrest to Abhishek Upadhyay who claimed he was vindictively booked under SC/ST Act by.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Tuesday granted interim protection from arrest to Abhishek Upadhyay who claimed he was vindictively booked under SC/ST Act by Ghaziabad police for an alleged road rage incident just because he had exposed embezzlement of donations offered by devotees at the Ram temple in Ayodhya.Appearing for the petitioner, senior advocate Pradeep Rai told a bench of CJI Surya Kant that Upadhyay was the whistleblower and the first to report the alleged misappropriation of monies donated by devotees at the Ayodhya temple.He said since UP Police is vindictive, investigations into the alleged road accident case lodged against him coupled with charges under SC/ST Act should be transferred to an independent agency such as CBI or Delhi Police.Rai complained that police are yet to furnish a copy of the FIR and CCTV camera footage of the alleged accident involving his vehicle and a two-wheeler to the petitioner who is accused of hurling caste-based abuses at the two-wheeler rider after the accident.The bench issued notice to Ghaziabad police and said that âno coercive action shall be taken against the petitioner in the FIR registered at Indirapuram police station, or any such subsequent FIR that may be registered against him in relation to the allegations.âAsking police to furnish a copy of the FIR to the petitioner to enable him to take remedial steps in accordance with the law, the bench said, âAs soon as a copy of the FIR is received by the petitioner, he shall be at liberty to approach the jurisdictional high court for seeking relevant relief.âGet the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: As Ukraine hits Russia's refineries, Russia targets Ukraine's petrol pumps
articles.summary: Fuel companies are urging customers not to linger at the pumps after a wave of deadly attacks.
articles.body:
"Fill up quickly and move on," Mayor Ihor Terekhov warns drivers in Ukraine's second largest city Kharkiv.

Two petrol stations in the city in Ukraine's north-east were hit by Russian drones on Monday, which local officials say wounded two people. In another attack on a petrol station outside the city of Kryvyi Rih last week, three people were killed.

Russia's campaign of targeting civilian filling stations with drones and missiles began in earnest in April, primarily in regions on the front line, and the attacks are steadily growing more frequent.

At the same time, Russia has endured two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries.

In total, Russia has hit at least 246 filling stations across Ukraine so far, says Oleksandr Sirenko, an analyst with Ukrainian energy think-tank Nafto Rynok ("Oil Market").

In July alone, the Centre for Information Resilience, an open-source investigation non-profit group, verified 114 Russian strikes on filling stations, compared with 66 the month before.

Given the threat, police have issued special guidance urging motorists to leave petrol stations and, if necessary, to abandon their vehicles whenever air raid alerts sound.

"You can fix your car, but you won't get your life back," says one police force in the Dnipropetrovsk region.

The damage is highly disruptive and puts civilians at considerable risk.

According to Sirenko, initially the attacks were being carried out with smaller, remote-controlled drones, but then Russia started using bigger, more expensive and more destructive Iranian-made Shahed drones.

One Shahed drone is estimated to cost between $20,000 (Â£14,500) and $50,000 (Â£36,000).

"One petrol station took five Shahed hits," Sirenko tells the BBC. "These Shaheds cost more than the petrol station."

Some key roads have no functioning petrol stations left, such as the road linking the two major cities of Kharkiv and Dnipro.

All the petrol stations have been destroyed around Opishnya, a large village in neighbouring Poltava region.

"You can see our enemy's strategy. They want to deprive us of fuel," says village chief Mykola Riznyk. In a video on Facebook, he says local authorities have begun stocking up on fuel, keeping small amounts of it in different locations.

In Mykolaiv in southern Ukraine, local resident and driver Kateryna Stokolya says petrol stations everywhere are becoming far stricter about not working during air alerts.

"Now everyone's making allowances for that, and it's not a problem," she tells the BBC. "Security comes first. If you can't fill up now, you'll fill up later. There are no queues or panic buying."

Stokolya believes that, in carrying out attacks of this nature, Russia's intended goal is "terrorising the public so we force the government to capitulate or accept agreements that do not favour Ukraine".

In Ukrainian-controlled areas of the partly occupied Kherson region, almost half the petrol stations have stopped working. The others get attacked by Russian drones "almost every day", says deputy regional administration head Oleksandr Tolokonnikov.

All petrol stations have reportedly been destroyed in Trostyanets, a town of almost 20,000 people near the north-eastern border with Russia. In response, local authorities started dispensing fuel straight from road tankers which keep changing their location to minimise the chances of being hit.

Ukrainians appear to be heeding the advice of authorities.

"Clients aren't browsing the aisles anymore, looking at what we've got on our shelves," says Oleksandr Melnychuk, head of the strategic marketing department at BRSM Nafta chain of petrol stations. "They fill up and are keen to get on their way as soon as possible."

His company has lost eight petrol stations and is rebuilding another two after they were hit.

To protect customers, BRSM Nafta has been building concrete shelters at its forecourts and also covering them in anti-drone nets. It has also shortened working hours and reduced the number of staff present in some locations.

However, so far the drone strikes have not had a dramatic impact on fuel supplies. According to a report by the National Bank of Ukraine, 4% of the country's filling stations have been damaged or destroyed, but the impact on the market has been small.

"Increasing sales in regions which are further away from the front line or from the border with Russia have made up for sales lost at destroyed stations," the report says.

The picture in Russia is very different, after Ukraine's campaign of attacks on Russian refineries and other infrastructure.

Russia has seen fuel shortages in almost every region as a result. One popular newspaper in Russia, Izvestia, said last week that petrol was only available at 28% of Russian filling stations.

Unlike in Russia, Ukraine does not rely on vulnerable large refineries and fuel depots, instead importing fuel by road using tanker trucks.

Ukraine's market is also saturated with numerous petrol stations, which usually offer drivers alternatives should one or several of them be targeted in a particular area, Sirenko says.

"You curse and drive on to another petrol station. OK, you travel for 10km more than you bargained for, but that's not such a big problem," he says.

If anything, it is the war between the US and Iran that is having a bigger impact on local fuel prices, he says. Normally, the most expensive parts of filling stations are left undamaged by Russian attacks, such as petrol and diesel tanks underground.

If anything, it is the war between the US and Iran that is having a bigger impact on local fuel prices, he says. Normally, the most expensive parts of filling stations are left undamaged by Russian attacks, such as petrol and diesel tanks underground.

UK missiles offer may help Ukraine - but they are not what Zelensky needs most

Burnham vows support for Ukraine despite 'outrageous threats' from Russia
paragraphs: "Fill up quickly and move on," Mayor Ihor Terekhov warns drivers in Ukraine's second largest city Kharkiv.

Two petrol stations in the city in Ukraine's north-east were hit by Russian drones on Monday, which local officials say wounded two people. In another attack on a petrol station outside the city of Kryvyi Rih last week, three people were killed.

Russia's campaign of targeting civilian filling stations with drones and missiles began in earnest in April, primarily in regions on the front line, and the attacks are steadily growing more frequent.
At the same time, Russia has endured two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries.
In total, Russia has hit at least 246 filling stations across Ukraine so far, says Oleksandr Sirenko, an analyst with Ukrainian energy think-tank Nafto Rynok ("Oil Market").
In July alone, the Centre for Information Resilience, an open-source investigation non-profit group, verified 114 Russian strikes on filling stations, compared with 66 the month before.
Given the threat, police have issued special guidance urging motorists to leave petrol stations and, if necessary, to abandon their vehicles whenever air raid alerts sound.
"You can fix your car, but you won't get your life back," says one police force in the Dnipropetrovsk region.
The damage is highly disruptive and puts civilians at considerable risk.

According to Sirenko, initially the attacks were being carried out with smaller, remote-controlled drones, but then Russia started using bigger, more expensive and more destructive Iranian-made Shahed drones.
One Shahed drone is estimated to cost between $20,000 (£14,500) and $50,000 (£36,000).
"One petrol station took five Shahed hits," Sirenko tells the BBC. "These Shaheds cost more than the petrol station."
Some key roads have no functioning petrol stations left, such as the road linking the two major cities of Kharkiv and Dnipro.
All the petrol stations have been destroyed around Opishnya, a large village in neighbouring Poltava region.

"You can see our enemy's strategy. They want to deprive us of fuel," says village chief Mykola Riznyk. In a video on Facebook, he says local authorities have begun stocking up on fuel, keeping small amounts of it in different locations.
In Mykolaiv in southern Ukraine, local resident and driver Kateryna Stokolya says petrol stations everywhere are becoming far stricter about not working during air alerts.
"Now everyone's making allowances for that, and it's not a problem," she tells the BBC. "Security comes first. If you can't fill up now, you'll fill up later. There are no queues or panic buying."

Stokolya believes that, in carrying out attacks of this nature, Russia's intended goal is "terrorising the public so we force the government to capitulate or accept agreements that do not favour Ukraine".

In Ukrainian-controlled areas of the partly occupied Kherson region, almost half the petrol stations have stopped working. The others get attacked by Russian drones "almost every day", says deputy regional administration head Oleksandr Tolokonnikov.

All petrol stations have reportedly been destroyed in Trostyanets, a town of almost 20,000 people near the north-eastern border with Russia. In response, local authorities started dispensing fuel straight from road tankers which keep changing their location to minimise the chances of being hit.
Ukrainians appear to be heeding the advice of authorities.

"Clients aren't browsing the aisles anymore, looking at what we've got on our shelves," says Oleksandr Melnychuk, head of the strategic marketing department at BRSM Nafta chain of petrol stations. "They fill up and are keen to get on their way as soon as possible."
His company has lost eight petrol stations and is rebuilding another two after they were hit.

To protect customers, BRSM Nafta has been building concrete shelters at its forecourts and also covering them in anti-drone nets. It has also shortened working hours and reduced the number of staff present in some locations.

However, so far the drone strikes have not had a dramatic impact on fuel supplies. According to a report by the National Bank of Ukraine, 4% of the country's filling stations have been damaged or destroyed, but the impact on the market has been small.
"Increasing sales in regions which are further away from the front line or from the border with Russia have made up for sales lost at destroyed stations," the report says.
The picture in Russia is very different, after Ukraine's campaign of attacks on Russian refineries and other infrastructure.
Russia has seen fuel shortages in almost every region as a result. One popular newspaper in Russia, Izvestia, said last week that petrol was only available at 28% of Russian filling stations.
Unlike in Russia, Ukraine does not rely on vulnerable large refineries and fuel depots, instead importing fuel by road using tanker trucks.
Ukraine's market is also saturated with numerous petrol stations, which usually offer drivers alternatives should one or several of them be targeted in a particular area, Sirenko says.
"You curse and drive on to another petrol station. OK, you travel for 10km more than you bargained for, but that's not such a big problem," he says.

If anything, it is the war between the US and Iran that is having a bigger impact on local fuel prices, he says. Normally, the most expensive parts of filling stations are left undamaged by Russian attacks, such as petrol and diesel tanks underground.

articles.title: Jeff Passan Rejects Conspiracy Theories of ‘Financial Fraud’ by Dodgers
articles.summary: Jeff Passan wasn't having it when a social media user questioned his coverage of the Dodgers.
articles.body:
An ESPN insider is speaking out against online theories that a reported federal probe into the owner of the Los Angeles Dodgers indicate wrongdoing by the team.

Jeff Passan sounded off on X, formerly Twitter , regarding the investigation into Mark Walter , the majority owner of the Boys in Blue who recently agreed to sell his Lakers ownership .

As Passan noted, the federal probe is into Walter's other businesses, and there's nothing to connect the Dodgers except the common ownership by Walter and his companies, Guggenheim Partners and TWG Global.

"I have no evidence — and no other media member has reported any — that the Dodgers did anything that ran afoul of the [collective bargaining agreement]," Passan responded to a user who critiqued his reporting. "Beyond that, the government is focused more on procedural questions — the mismarking of affiliated investments and the web of companies under Guggenheim's umbrella — than anything specifically related to the Dodgers."

Passan defends his reporting — and himself

That user took issue with what Passan called "the full story that helps separate fact from fiction" and suggested that the reporter "acknowledge your own naivete in declaring that the Dodgers 'cracked the system.'"

"That was the phrase that had most of baseball twitter roasting you," they wrote. "All you had to say was financial fraud does not equal cracking the system, but alas, your ego got in the way."

"You are well within your rights to assume whatever you want to assume, and if you want to suggest there was some kind of fraud that specifically impacted on-field performance, you do you," he wrote. "I'm not going to do that because I have no idea how the money they received from selling the debt on their TV network, for example, was used. I wasn't being naive when I said the Dodgers cracked the system. They did."

Passan detailed that the Dodgers "recognized that cash is a grand separator in terms of securing talent," but that's not all it takes to win.

"You know who else did? The Mets . And they stunk. Every billionaire has access to cash. Not as much as the Dodgers, certainly, but if they want to get more capital to invest in their team, they can. They choose not to," Passan said. "And that is well within their rights, too, but to suggest that because Mark Walter is under investigation for one business' tactics that it automatically ties into another's — with zero hard evidence showing that's the case — is simply a case of you fitting what you think you know to a conclusion you already made."

articles.title: Instagram CEO denies company hid low use of teen safety feature in Meta trial
articles.summary: Adam Mosseri is first top executive from Meta to testify in blockbuster lawsuit brought by 29 US states
articles.body:
Instagram's CEO disputed allegations by US prosecutors that his company hid negative information from the public while testifying during a blockbuster social media trial.

"I am not trying to encourage my team to hide anything," the CEO, Adam Mosseri, told a California courtroom on Tuesday.

Mosseri is the first top executive from Meta, which owns both Instagram and Facebook, to testify in a historic lawsuit brought by 29 US states. His testimony began toward the end of the day on Tuesday and is slated to continue on Wednesday.

When the executive was posed with multiple questions about not disclosing low user numbers for Instagram's features geared toward teen safety, he brushed them aside, saying: "We don't publish every single stat."

Jason Slothouber, a prosecutor for the state of Colorado, asked specifically about a tool called Take a Break, meant to encourage teens to close Instagram if they'd been scrolling for a while. Slothouber pointed out that just 1.8% of teens signed up for the feature, and that while Mosseri had touted the tool, he never publicly disclosed that number.

"I've definitely said publicly that the opt-in rates are low," Mosseri responded. "I don't know if I've said numbers."

The jury trial, taking place in federal court in Oakland, California, began with opening statements last week. The lawsuit centers on the states' allegations that Meta deliberately designed addictive products that hooked young people, leading to mental health issues, including anxiety, depression and suicide. The states additionally claim the social media company regularly collected data on children under the age of 13 without parental permission in violation of federal and state laws.

If found liable, Meta could be forced to pay damages as high as $200bn and change the design of its products to make them safer for kids. Legal experts say the outcome of this trial could fundamentally change the way social media apps function for young people.

Meta has denied all allegations, saying the states are chasing an "outlandish payout". A spokesperson said Tuesday that Meta's safety teams strive to be industry-leading and that Mosseri's testimony showed the company does research to find ways to improve user experience.

Mosseri became the head of Instagram in 2018 and over the years has faced scrutiny about whether he may have dismissed internal warnings about the platform's addictive design and negative effects on young people. He was called to testify before a Senate committee in December 2021 and as a witness in other trials about the alleged harm of social media to children.

On Tuesday, Slothouber asked Mosseri about a blog post he had published just one day before his Senate testimony. The post was titled "raising the standard for protecting teens and supporting parents online" and included the announcement of the Take a Break tool. Slothouber questioned Mosseri about the timing of his post.

"We had made progress, and we wanted to get the progress out, so we could talk about the progress," Mosseri responded.

Slothouber then asked the CEO whether he was aware of the phrase "drumbeat messaging", the idea of saying something repeatedly until it's drummed into people's heads. Mosseri said he had and that it's necessary when dealing with parents and safety features. "We need to repeat it to raise awareness of those tools," Mosseri testified.

Over the last week, jurors also heard from Arturo Béjar , a former Meta safety engineer turned whistleblower, who testified that the company has a "don't ask, don't tell" strategy when it comes to the safety of children on its platforms. They also heard from a psychologist and other former and current company employees.

The trial is expected to last through September with several other witnesses, including Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

articles.title: Bears Camp Report: Darnell Wright injured, Corners return, Jordan van den Berg with the ones, and more
articles.summary: There was a lot going on at the Bears practice at Halas Hall today. @wiltfongjr shares some news here.
articles.body:
The Chicago Bears held their final training camp practice in front of the fans today at Halas Hall, and before they got into a red zone period, cornerback Jaylon Johnson brought the team together for a meeting with the message that the practice wasn't good enough. The message was heard as tight end Cole Kmet said in his post-practice presser, "I thought it ended up being one of our better practices through camp so far."

A strong finish for the nearly 2-hour practice before what will likely be a light workout tomorrow and a joint practice with the Tennessee Titans on Thursday. The Bears play the Titans to close the preseason slate on Saturday.

The Bears could be without a few players the rest of the week, as several left today with an injury, most notably starting right tackle Darnell Wright , who exited to Halas Hall with trainers as he flexed his right arm. That's the same arm he injured last season, so hopefully there's good news coming about that.

Defensive tackle Gervon Dexter Sr. also left with an injury, and in case you missed it, he was at the center of a trade rumor today . Tight end Hayden Large was sidelined with a left arm issue, and cornerback Dontae Manning also left practice and did not return.

Running back Kyle Monangai is still week-to-week, new defensive end Marcus Davenport wasn't practicing, and defensive end Austin Booker , who missed Saturday's game in Cincinnati , was also not participating.

However, the Bears did get some good news on the injury front. Safety Elijah Hicks and rookie linebacker Keyshaun Elliott were activated from the PUP list, and both got in some work. Quarterback Tyson Bagent returned after missing last week with a hamstring issue. Cornerback Tyrique Stevenson was back in team drills, starting along with Jaylon Johnson. Backup corners Terell Smith and Jaylon Jones were also back, but neither did team drills. Left tackle Ozzy Trapilo was suited up but still just doing individual drills.

Rookie DT Jordan van den Berg was working some with the starters.

With Booker not practicing, Jamree Kromah was getting some work with the ones. ( link )

Defensive lineman James Lynch also spent time with the first team.

While head coach Ben Johnson said at his pre-practice press conference that they are still trying to figure out left tackle, Braxton Jones was with the ones most of the day. "From the angle I had, looked like LT Braxton Jones did a nice job in 9-on-7 period," shared Brad Biggs. "For the snaps he was in, there sure was an emphasis to run to his side. Three of the four D'Andre Swift runs went for nice gains."

Theo Benedet went in with the ones at right tackle with Wright out.

Cam Lewis got most of the work at safety next to rookie Dillon Thieneman. Ben Johnson said this morning that the safety spot next to the rookie is also an uncertainty.

Someone check the wind, because Zack Pearson shared that " Cairo Santos just drained a 59-yard field goal."

They closed practice with a long drive drill to test their cardio (link), and safety Xavier Woods ended practice by intercepting Case Keenum .

Per CHGO's Adam Hoge, defensive tackle Grady Jarrett yelled "Get up!" at d-linemen Jordan van den Berg and Montez Sweat when both were on a knee during the long drive drill.

Quarterback Caleb Williams and the first team offense had a mix of good and bad throughout the day. Williams moved the offense from its own 1 yard line when he found Rome Odunze down the middle for a big gain on third down. But Williams then completed one of his six pass attempts during a 7-on-7 drill — one of those were a drop by running back D'Andre Swift. The first team offense had a good red zone period working from the defense's 14 yard line. Williams found Odunze once again for a touchdown pass before Swift ran in 14 yards for another touchdown on the following play.

articles.title: Kinley Rasmus breaks the record for hits by a girl at the Little League World Series
articles.summary: Kinley Rasmus is on a record-setting roll at the Little League World Series.  The 12-year-old pitcher and shortstop for the Phenix City, Alabama, team repres...
articles.body:
WILLIAMSPORT, Pa. (AP) — Kinley Rasmus is on a record-setting roll at the Little League World Series.

The 12-year-old pitcher and shortstop for the Phenix City, Alabama, team representing the Southeast at the tournament had a pair of hits during a comeback win over a team from Tacoma, Washington, on Tuesday that kept Phenix City's season alive.

Rasmus has five hits during the double-elimination tournament, the most by a girl at the Little League World Series.

The daughter of former major league pitcher Cory Rasmus has already distinguished herself on the mound. Kinley Rasmus allowed one hit in six innings in a game against Tacoma earlier in the tournament. The eight strikeouts she recorded in that outing tied Mo'Ne Davis' mark for strikeouts by a girl in a game.

Rasmus then added six more strikeouts in a victory on Monday to boost her tournament total to 14, also tying a record held by Davis.

She will have a chance to add to her hit total when Phenix City plays another elimination game on Wednesday.
